\begin{frame}
\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
\begin{block}{The question}
Swifts return to the same roofs every spring, but the roofs are being
replaced. Volunteers counted the birds entering each street's eaves at
dusk, every evening for six weeks, to learn which streets still hold
colonies and which have lost them since the last count a decade ago.
\end{block}
\begin{block}{How the counts were made}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Two counters per street, one at each end.
  \item Counts in five-minute bins from sunset.
  \item A street counted at least three times.
\end{itemize}
\end{block}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
\begin{block}{What was found}
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
  \toprule
  \textbf{Street} & \textbf{Then} & \textbf{Now} \\
  \midrule
  Mill Lane & 42 & 38 \\
  Church Row & 27 & 9 \\
  High Street & 15 & 0 \\
  \bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{block}
\begin{block}{A colony's decline}
With $n_0$ birds at the first count and a yearly loss $r$, a colony
counted $t$ years later holds
\[ n_t = n_0 (1 - r)^t , \]
so Church Row's fall from 27 to 9 in ten years is a loss of about one
bird in ten each year.
\end{block}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
\begin{block}{Where they nest}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth, alt={Three coloured rectangles for
three rows of eaves}]{../corpus/rects.png}
\end{block}
\begin{alertblock}{What can be done}
Nest boxes fitted under new eaves were occupied within two seasons on
every street that tried them. The cheapest intervention is to leave the
old gaps open when a roof is repaired.
\end{alertblock}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
